'''''Acacia mearnsii''''', commonly known as '''black wattle''', '''late black wattle''' or '''green wattle''',<ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Kodela |first1=Phillip G. |title=''Acacia mearnsii'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Acacia%20mearnsii |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=26 September 2020}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Fabaceae]] and is [[Endemism|endemic]] to south-eastern Australia. It is usually an erect tree with smooth bark, [[Glossary of leaf morphology#bipinnate|bipinnate]] leaves and spherical heads of fragrant pale yellow or cream-coloured flowers followed by black to reddish brown [[legume (fruit)|pods]]. In some other parts of the world, it is regarded as an [[invasive species]].

==Description==
''Acacis mearnsii'' is a spreading shrub or erect tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|10|m}} and has smooth bark, sometimes corrugated at the base of old specimens. The leaves are bipinnate with 7 to 31 pairs of [[Glossary of botanical terms#pinna|pinnae]], each with 25 to 78 pairs of [[Leaflet (botany)|pinnules]]. There is a spherical [[Gland (botany)|gland]] up to {{cvt|8|mm}} below the lowest pair of pinnae. The scented flowers are arranged in spherical heads of 20 to 40, pale yellow or cream-coloured, with the heads on hairy [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]] {{cvt|2–8|mm|2}} long. Flowering mainly occurs from October to December and black to reddish-brown pods, {{cvt|30–150|mm}} long and {{cvt|4.5–8|mm}} wide develop from October to February.<ref name="ABRS" /><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Kodela |first1=Phillip G. |title=''Acacia mearnsii'' De Wild. |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Acacia~mearnsii |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=26 September 2020}}</ref><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |title=''Acacia mearnsii'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/a72a846c-7a92-4a4a-8dca-e2582a0f393e |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=26 September 2020}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Belgian naturalist [[Émile Auguste Joseph De Wildeman]] described the black wattle in 1925 in his book ''Plantae Bequaertianae''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Acacia mearnsii''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/474527|publisher=APNI|access-date=26 September 2020}}</ref> The species is named after American naturalist [[Edgar Alexander Mearns]], who collected the type from a cultivated specimen in East [[Africa]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/euctax.pl?/PlantNet/wattle=&name=Acacia+mearnsii|title=WattleWeb – Acacia mearnsii|last=Tame|first=Terry|author2=Phillip Kodela|author3=Barry Conn|author4=Ken Hill|date=June 2001|publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney|access-date=21 October 2008|archive-date=10 July 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090710200459/http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/euctax.pl?%2FPlantNet%2Fwattle=&name=Acacia+mearnsii}}</ref> Along with other bipinnate wattles, it is classified in the section ''Botrycephalae'' within the subgenus ''Phyllodineae'' in the genus ''Acacia''. An analysis of genomic and chloroplast DNA along with morphological characters found that the section is polyphyletic, though the close relationships of many species were unable to be resolved. ''Acacia mearnsii '' appears to be most closely related to ''[[Acacia dealbata|A. dealbata]]'', ''[[Acacia nanodealbata|A. nanodealbata]]'' and ''[[Acacia baileyana|A. baileyana]]''.<ref name="brown 1991">{{cite journal|date=1991|title=Bipinnate acacias (Acacia subg. Phyllodineae sect. Botrycephalae) of eastern Australia are polyphyletic based on DNA sequence data |author1=Brown, Gillian K. |author2=Ariati, Siti R. |author3=Murphy, Daniel J. |author4=Miller, Joseph T. H. |author5=Ladiges, Pauline Y. |journal=Australian Systematic Botany|volume=19|issue=4|pages=315–26|doi=10.1071/SB05039}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''A. mearnsii'' is native to south-eastern [[Australia]] and [[Tasmania]], but has been introduced to [[North America]], [[South America]], [[Asia]], [[Europe]], [[List of islands in the Pacific Ocean|Pacific]] and [[List of islands in the Indian Ocean|Indian Ocean]] islands, [[Africa]], and [[New Zealand]].<ref name="pier" /><ref name="adair">Adair, R. (2002). Black Wattle: South Africa Manages Conflict of Interest. CABI Biocontrol News March 2002, Volume 23 No. 1. [http://pest.cabweb.org/Journals/BNI/Bni23-1/Gennews.htm web] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050404234030/http://pest.cabweb.org/Journals/BNI/Bni23-1/Gennews.htm |date=4 April 2005 }}</ref><ref name="paiva">Paiva, J. 1999. Acacia. In Talavera, S. Aedo, C, Castroviejo, S, Romero Zarco, C, Sáez, L, Salgueiro, F.J & Velayos, (ed). Flora Iberica – Plantas Vasculares de la Península Ibérica e Islas Baleares. Vol.VII(I). Leguminosae. Real Jardín Botánico, CSIS. Madrid. {{ISBN|84-00-06221-3}}. pp. 11- 25.</ref><ref name="franco71">Franco, J.A. 1971. Nova Flora de Portugal (Continente e Açores). Vol. 1. Franco, J.A. (Ed.). Lisboa.</ref><ref name="tutin">Tutin, T. G., Heywood, V.H., Burges, N.A., Moore, D.M., Valentine, D.H., Walters, S.M. & Webb, D.A. 1992. Flora Europaea. Vol.2 Rosaceae to Umbelliferae. (reprint). Cambridge University Press. Cambridge. {{ISBN|0-521-06662-X}}, pp. 84–85</ref> In these areas it is often used as a commercial source of [[tannin]] or a source of firewood for local communities.

In some regions, introduced plants of this species are considered a weed. This is because they threaten native [[habitat]]s by competing with indigenous vegetation, replacing grass communities, reducing native [[biodiversity]] and increasing water loss from [[riparian zone]]s. In Africa, ''A. mearnsii'' competes with local vegetation for nitrogen and water resources, which are particularly scarce in certain regions, endangering the livelihoods of millions of people.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Jose|first1=Shibu|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nPGci6i1ZT8C&q=Plant+Ecology|title=Invasive Plant Ecology|last2=Singh|first2=Harminder Pal|last3=Batish|first3=Daizy Rani|last4=Kohli|first4=Ravinder Kumar|publisher=CRC Press|year=2013|isbn=978-1-4398-8126-2|page=2|language=en}}</ref>

In its native range ''A. mearnsii'' is a tree of tall woodland and forests in subtropical and warm temperate regions. In Africa the species grows in disturbed areas, range/[[grassland]]s, riparian zones, urban areas, water courses, and [[wikt:mesic|mesic]] habitats at an altitude of between {{convert|600|and|1700|m}}. In Africa it grows in a range of [[climate]]s including warm temperate dry climates and moist tropical climates. ''A. mearnsii'' is reported to tolerate an annual [[precipitation (meteorology)|precipitation]] of between {{convert|66|and|228|cm|abbr=on}}, an annual mean temperature of {{convert|14.7|to|27.8|C}}, and a pH of 5.0–7.2.<ref name="duke">Duke, J. A. 1983. Acacia mearnsii. Handbook of Energy Crops. Unpublished. [http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/duke_energy/Acacia_mearnsii.html web]</ref>  ''A. mearnsii'' does not grow well on very dry and poor soils.<ref name="franco43">Franco, J.A. 1943. Dendrologia Florestal. Lisboa.</ref>

==Ecology in Australia==
''A. mearnsii'' plays an important role in the native ecosystem of Australia. As a [[Ecological succession|pioneer plant]] it quickly binds the [[Erosion|erosion-prone]] soil following the [[Wildfire|bushfires]] that are common in its Australian habitats. Like other [[Fabaceae|leguminous plants]], it [[Nitrogen fixation|fixes atmospheric nitrogen]] in the soil. Other woodland species can rapidly use these increased nitrogen levels provided by the nodules of bacteria present in their expansive root systems. Hence they play a critical part in the natural regeneration of Australian bushland after fires.

[[Image:Starr 050816-7454 Acacia mearnsii.jpg|thumb|right|200px|''Acacia mearnsii'' seed pods]]
* Consumption and excretion: The seeds are potentially distributed by [[rodent]]s or birds.<ref name="carr">Carr, G. D. Acacia mearnsii University of Hawaii, Botany Department. [http://www.botany.hawaii.edu/faculty/carr/aca_mea.htm web]</ref>
* For ornamental purposes (local)
* By animals: The dispersal of the seeds of ''A . mearnsii'' is believed to be aided by cattle and birds.<ref name="milton">Milton, S.J., Dean W.R.J. and Richardson, D.M. 2003. Economic Incentives for Restoring Natural Capital in Southern African Rangelands, Front Ecol Environ+C26 1 (5): 247,254.</ref>
* By people: Local people collecting branches and logs for firewood may spread seeds.<ref name="sankaran">Sankaran, K. V. (2002). Black Wattle Problem Emerges in Indian Forests. CABI Biocontrol News March 2002 23(1) [https://web.archive.org/web/20050404234030/http://pest.cabweb.org/Journals/BNI/Bni23-1/Gennews.htm web page (archived 2005)]</ref>
** Transportation of soil: The seeds may also be spread by the movement of seed-contaminated soil.<ref name="dewit">De Wit, M.P., Crookes, D.J. and Van Wilgen, B.W. 2001. Conflicts of Interest in Environmental Management: Estimating the Costs and Benefits of a Tree Invasion, Biological Invasions: 3 167 – 178.</ref>
* By water: The hard-coated seeds are spread readily down water courses.<ref name="dewit"/>

[[Koala]]s use tree-hugging for cooling in very hot weather: they have been found to favour the non-food ''A. mearnsii'' to eucalypts for this purpose.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Briscoe |first1=Natalie J. |last2=Handasyde |first2=Kathrine A. |last3=Griffiths |first3=Stephen R. |last4=Porter |first4=Warren P. |last5=Krockenberger |first5=Andrew |last6=Kearney |first6=Michael R. |title=Tree-hugging koalas demonstrate a novel thermoregulatory mechanism for arboreal mammals |journal=Biology Letters |date=30 June 2014 |volume=10 |issue=6 |article-number=20140235 |doi=10.1098/rsbl.2014.0235|pmc=4090547 }}</ref>

[[Mycorrhiza|Mycorrhizal fungi]] attach to the roots to produce food for [[marsupial]] animals, and these animals in turn disperse the spores in their droppings to perpetuate the symbiotic relationship between the wattle's roots and mycorrhizal fungi.

The cracks and crevices in the wattle's bark are home for many insects and invertebrates. The rare [[Pseudalmenus chlorinda myrsilus|Tasmanian hairstreak]] butterfly lays her eggs in these cracks, which hatch to produce caterpillar larva attended by ants (''[[Iridomyrmex]]'' sp.) that feed off the sweet exudates from the larva.{{Citation needed|date=November 2017}} ''A. mearnsii'' is used similarly as a larval host plant and food source by the imperial hairstreak, ''[[Jalmenus evagoras]]''.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Biology of Australian butterflies|date=1999|publisher=CSIRO Pub|others=Kitching, R. L. (Roger Laurence), 1945-, CSIRO (Australia)|isbn=978-0-643-05027-3|location=Collingwood, VIC, Australia|oclc=40792921}}</ref>

The tree is home to various grubs, such as wood moths, which provide a food source to black cockatoos, which strip the bark for access to these borers.

During winter, insects, birds and marsupials are hosted by the black wattle with the aid of their supplies of [[nectar]] in their leaf axials. These creatures provide an important predatory role to deal with tree dieback caused by scarab beetles and pasture pests.

Black wattles, along with gums, native box and native hop form the framework vegetation on so-called "hill-topping" sites. They often constitute isolated remnant pockets of native vegetation amongst a lower sea of exotic pasture. These "hill-topping" sites are critical habitat for male butterflies to attract females for mating, which then lay their eggs under the wattle's bark elsewhere but still within close proximity. It's the only acceptable mating site in the area for these butterflies.

Black wattle flowers provide very [[nitrogen]]-rich pollen with no nectar. They attract pollen-feeding birds, such as [[wattlebird]]s, [[yellow-throated honeyeater]]s and [[New Holland honeyeater]]s. The protein-rich nectar in the leaf axials is very sustaining for nurturing the growth of juvenile nestlings and young invertebrates, e.g. ants.

[[Ant]]s harvest the seed, attracted by the fleshy, oil-rich [[elaiosome]] (or seed stalk), which they bury and store in widely dispersed locations. These seeds are buried ready for germinating with the next soaking rains. However, a "wattle seed-eating insect" which enjoys liquid meals using its proboscis-like injector to pierce the [[wikt:testa|testa]] and suck out the embryo, often reduces the seed's viability.<ref>Australian Plants Society (Tasmania), June 2000</ref>

==Status as an invasive species==
In some parts of the world, ''A. mearnsii'' is considered to be an invasive species. Its invasiveness is due to its production of large numbers of seeds each year and to its large [[Crown (botany)|crown]] that shades other species.<ref name="GISD">{{cite web |title=''Acacia mearnsii'' |url=http://www.iucngisd.org/gisd/speciesname/Acacia+mearnsii |publisher=Global Invasive Species Database |access-date=26 September 2020}}</ref>

In [[South Africa]], it is listed as a Category 2 invader in the National Environmental Biodiversity Management Act. This means a permit is required to handle a species and ensure it does not spread beyond the area of the permit.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=South African Government Gazette: Number 37320 |url=https://archive.gazettes.africa/archive/za/2014/za-government-gazette-dated-2014-02-12-no-37320.pdf |journal=South Africa Government Gazette |volume=584 |page=8}}</ref>

In the [[European Union]], it is included in the [[list of invasive alien species of Union concern]] and hence cannot be imported, bred, transported, commercialized, or intentionally released into the environment in any of its member states.<ref>{{Cite web |title=List of Invasive Alien Species of Union concern |url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02016R1141-20250807 |date=7 August 2025 |access-date=29 March 2026|website=eur-lex.europa.eu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Regulation No. 1143/2014 of the European parliament and of the council of 22 October 2014 on the prevention and management of the introduction and spread of invasive alien species |url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32014R1143&from=EN |publisher=European Union |date=2014-11-04 |location=Strasbourg |access-date=2026-03-29 |archive-date=2017-03-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170303185733/http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32014R1143&from=EN |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Uses==
The [[Ngunnawal]] people of the [[Australian Capital Territory]] use the gum as food and to make cement (when mixed with ash), and to ensure a supply of sap, the bark was cut in the autumn.<ref name=ngunn/> The bark was also used to make coarse rope and string, and used to be infused in water to make a medicine for indigestion.<ref name=ngunn>Ngunnawal Elders (2014) 'Ngunnawal Plant Use.' ACT Government: Canberra</ref>

==Reproduction==
''A. mearnsii'' produces copious numbers of small seeds that are not dispersed actively. The species may resprout from basal shoots following a fire.<ref name="pier">PIER, 2003. Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk [http://www.hear.org/pier/species/acacia_mearnsii.htm web]</ref> It also generates numerous suckers that result in thickets consisting of clones.<ref name="pier"/> Seeds may remain viable for up to 50 years.<ref name="wessa">{{cite web|url=http://www.geocities.com/wessaaliens/species/bwattle.htm |title=Alien Invader Plants |year=2002 |access-date=22 October 2008 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20091024144312/http://www.geocities.com/wessaaliens/species/bwattle.htm |archive-date=24 October 2009 }}</ref>
